The width of the confidence intervals stems largely from uncertainty at each time horizon. For the one-day forecast, the interval is relatively narrow (410.0 to 427.0) because the data or conditions from prior days typically dominate short-term movements, leaving little room for unexpected behavior. For the one-week horizon, the interval widens substantially, reflecting the fact that small cumulative deviations from expectations can grow over several days. By one month, the interval is even wider (370.0 to 490.0), capturing the increasing variability that arises as more unpredictable factors—such as economic changes, policy shifts, or unexpected external shocks—come into play the further out we forecast. Essentially, the longer the time frame, the more uncertainties compound, leading to a wider range of possible outcomes.

Specific risks or events could drive actual outcomes outside the stated intervals, though such instances would likely be rare or extreme. At the one-month horizon, larger systemic risks—such as unexpected regulatory actions, major economic shifts, or disruptive technological developments—could push outcomes outside the forecast range. These types of events are rare and challenging to predict but could cause significant deviations from the expected range, especially at longer time scales where their impacts have more time to materialize.
